head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dict from token id to its expiry time
Hash map for O(1) lookup by key
A token generated or renewed now expires ttl later
tokenId in self.exp and self.exp[tokenId] > currentTime
Renew only unexpired tokens (an expired token cannot be renewed; expiry at exactly currentTime counts as expired)
sum(1 for e in …values() if e > currentTime)
Counts tokens whose expiry is still in the future

p: `timeToLive = 5`:

Time only moves forward, so a token stays expired once expired, and `renew` ignores it. Leaving it in the dict is correct; cleaning it up would only save memory. Counting scans all stored tokens: O(n). A heap or an ordered dict would make the count cheaper.

1797.takeaway: Dict of token → expiry time; renew only if still unexpired, and count expiries strictly in the future.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sum of |nums1[i] − nums2[i]| before any change
Sorted copy of nums1 for binary search: the replacement may be ANY element of nums1
Insertion position of b in the sorted list; the closest values to b are at i and i − 1
How much replacing this position's value reduces its difference
Apply the single best replacement, then reduce modulo as required

blocks.h: Why only one replacement and why binary search?
p: Exactly one replacement is allowed at most, so the answer is the total minus the single largest reduction. For a position with target b, the best replacement is the value in nums1 nearest to b, found by binary search in the sorted copy rather than by scanning all n values.

1818.takeaway: Total difference minus the best single improvement; the best replacement value is the nearest to nums2[i], found by bisect.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum side jumps to be in lane 1, 2, 3 at the current point; the frog starts in lane 2 (cost 0) and reaching lane 1 or 3 costs one jump
An obstacle blocks that lane at this point
You can jump from the cheapest open lane into any other free lane at this point for one extra jump

p: `obstacles = [0,1,2,3,0]` (the value is the blocked lane at that point, 0 for none):

head: point
obstacle lane
dp = jumps to be in lanes 1, 2, 3

blocks.h: Why can sideways jumps be treated as a single step?
p: At the same point the frog may jump between any two lanes without obstacles for a cost of one (it can jump directly between the lanes 1 and 3 as well), so the new cost of a free lane is at most (cheapest other lane) + 1. One pass of `min(dp[l], m + 1)` suffices.

1824.takeaway: Three-lane DP: block the obstacle lane, then every free lane costs at most (cheapest lane) + 1.

What it does

Length of the run (the group is an iterator and must be consumed)
A window of five consecutive runs
The five runs spell a, e, i, o, u in order: a beautiful substring made of whole runs

p: `"aeiaaioaaaaeiiiiouuuooaauuaeiu"`: windows of five runs that spell `aeiou`:

A beautiful substring must contain all five vowels in nondecreasing order, so it consists of exactly five runs a, e, i, o, u in this order (no run can repeat or be skipped). Working on runs makes each window a constant-size check.

1839.takeaway: Compress into runs with groupby and look for five consecutive runs spelling a-e-i-o-u.

p: `[[1993,1999],[2000,2010]]`; only years where the difference changes are shown:
Adding 1 to every year in each lifespan would cost O(years) per person. Marking only the endpoints and taking a prefix sum applies all lifespans in a single O(years) pass.

1854.takeaway: Difference array over years (+1 at birth, −1 at death) then a prefix sum for the population.

blocks.h: Why a plain simulation is fast enough
p: The total leaked after t seconds is t(t+1)/2, which grows quadratically, so the loop runs at most about √(2·(memory1 + memory2)) times, around 2·10⁴ for the largest inputs.

1860.takeaway: Simulate: leak t bytes into the stick with more memory (stick 1 on ties) until neither has room.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Bitwise OR of all numbers: a bit is set if any number has it
Combining the bits that appear anywhere
Shift left as multiplication by a power of two

bullets: Answer 28 = the sum of the XOR of all 8 subsets.

p: Look at one bit position. If no number has that bit, it contributes 0. If at least one has it, exactly half of all 2^n subsets contain an odd number of numbers with that bit, so the bit is set in the XOR of 2^(n−1) subsets and contributes (bit value) × 2^(n−1). Summing over bits gives OR × 2^(n−1).

1863.takeaway: Each bit that appears in any number is set in exactly half the subsets' XOR: answer = (OR of all) << (n − 1).

What it does

A rhombus of size 0 is a single cell
while i - k >= 0 and i + k < m and …
Grows the rhombus (a diamond with centre (i, j) and 'radius' k) while all four corners stay inside the grid
Walks the four edges of the diamond; each edge contributes k cells starting at a different corner, so every border cell is counted once

p: For the 5×5 grid, rhombuses centred at the middle cell (2, 2):
bullets: All rhombus sums plus every single cell are collected; the three largest distinct values are `[228, 216, 211]`.

p: The problem sums the border cells of each rhombus, not its interior. Walking the four sides with a loop of k steps per side adds each border cell exactly once (each side starts at its own corner and stops before the next corner).

bullets: Time: O(m · n · min(m, n)²): each cell tries up to min(m, n)/2 sizes, each costing O(k).

1878.takeaway: Enumerate every centre and radius, sum the four edges of the diamond, and keep the three largest distinct sums.

Shortest path in an unweighted grid

p: A 5×5 maze (`.` open, `+` wall), entrance at (1, 0), whose only exit is the open bottom cell (4, 3). Cells entered by BFS in order with their distance:

blocks.h: Why mark the entrance as a wall at the start?
p: The entrance is on the border and open, so without marking it, the search would count it as an exit at distance 0 or revisit it. Turning it into '+' makes it a wall for all later steps.

1926.takeaway: BFS from the entrance; the first open border cell reached is the nearest exit.

p: `nums + nums` builds a new list and leaves the original unchanged. `nums += nums` would extend the original in place (still correct here, but it mutates the caller's list). The problem asks for a new array, so `+` is the safe choice.

1929.takeaway: Concatenate the list with itself using + to get a new array.

What it does

Heights to the right that could still be seen by someone further left, decreasing from bottom to top
while st and st[-1] < heights[i]: pop; ans += 1
Each shorter person is visible to i, and is then hidden by i for everyone further left
The first person who is at least as tall blocks the view beyond them but is still visible

p: `[10,6,8,5,11,9]` scanned right to left:

blocks.h: Why can popped people be discarded?
p: If person i is taller than a person to the right, then for anyone standing left of i, that shorter person is hidden behind i. They will never be visible to anyone further left, so they can leave the stack.

bullets: Time: O(n), each height is pushed and popped once.

1944.takeaway: Monotonic stack scanning right to left: count the shorter people popped, plus one for the first taller one.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: h = [-p for p in piles]; heapify(h)
Python's heap is a min-heap, so storing negatives makes the largest pile come out first (max-heap trick)
Priority queue with the largest item first
Negates the sum of negatives back to the total

blocks.h: Why always take from the largest pile?
p: The number of stones removed from a pile is floor(x/2), which grows with x. Taking from the largest pile removes the most stones this step. The largest pile after halving may still be the largest, which the heap handles.

1962.takeaway: Max-heap (negated min-heap): repeatedly halve the largest pile k times.

What it does

Alternates a small value from the lower half with a large value from the upper half

bullets: Result `[1, 4, 2, 5, 3]`: every interior element differs from its neighbours' average (True).

p: The result alternates small, large, small, large. An interior small value is smaller than both neighbours (large values), so it cannot equal their average, and an interior large value is larger than both neighbours, same argument. Distinct values in the sorted halves guarantee the strict inequality.

1968.takeaway: Sort, then interleave the lower and upper halves so every element is a strict peak or valley.

What it does

rows: An odd length can't be an array plus its doubles
Smallest value first: it can't be the double of anything still unused, so it must be an original
0's double is 0, so zeros pair with each other and need an even count
Not enough doubles to pair with all copies of x

p: `[1,3,4,2,6,8]`, values in ascending order:

The smallest remaining value can only be an original (its half would be smaller and was already removed or doesn't exist). Pairing it with its double forces the choice, and the rest follows by repetition.

2007.takeaway: Greedy from the smallest: each value is an original, so remove its doubles; zeros need an even count.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Smallest value seen so far (to the left)
x > lo: best = max(best, x - lo)
A larger later value gives a valid increasing pair (i < j and nums[i] < nums[j])
x ≤ lo: x is the new minimum, no pair is formed
The answer when no increasing pair exists

blocks.h: Why is a running minimum enough?
p: For each j, the best i < j is the smallest earlier value. Keeping that minimum as we scan gives the best partner in O(1). Equal values do not count, as the problem needs a strictly smaller earlier element.

2016.takeaway: Running minimum: best difference = max(x − minimum so far) over later x larger than it.
